Abstract
Fog and edge computing bring computational resources closer to end users, which is necessary for the rapid growth of 
applications that are latency-sensitive and bandwidth-intensive. The service placement is a significant issue since optimiz­
ing it depends on several dynamic variables, including the network’s topology, heterogeneity, and available resources. 
These issues are challenging due to their high level of complexity, which is why Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven solu­
tions are so appealing. In this article, we present a systematic literature review for service placement strategies in fog and 
edge computing environments that use heuristic optimization, reinforcement learning, and deep learning for optimization. 
Further, we propose a comprehensive taxonomy to thoroughly categorize and evaluate current methods according to per­
formance indicators like energy usage, latency reduction, network utilization, quality of service, and general workload 
flexibility. Additionally, this work establishes a correlation between metric priority and methodological trends throughout 
the research period. One of our main contributions is the methodical categorization and critical evaluation of heuristic 
approaches, which shows how they are changing in their ability to balance computational efficiency and solution quality, 
especially in dynamic, large-scale edge contexts and multi-objective optimization. This paper acts as a guide for profes­
sionals and practitioners in the rapidly evolving field of AI-based service placement solutions and highlights new direc­
tions to help define future research topics.

Service placement is challenged by a number of unique 
factors introduced by the dynamic nature, coupled with 
heterogeneous fog/edge environments [7]. One of those 
challenges deals with edge devices differing computational 
abilities as well as imposing limitations that affect the per­
formance and scalability of deployed services. Moreover, 
IoT devices can move around while network conditions 
vary. Hence, there is a need for adaptive real-time placement 
strategies that guarantee continuous service quality [10]. 
Additionally, edge devices produce large volumes of data. 
Data management and storage strategies may further com­
plicate the problem posed by service placement, among oth­
ers. The services may be anything, such as runtime, storage, 
application, etc. In cloud computing, a centralized approach 
will be used, and cloud will provide requested resources to 
the end users [11]. But in fog/edge computing, the scenario 
is quite different, because services will be provided by fog/
edge nodes that are nearby of the user.
One of the significant challenges in fog/edge computing 
environments is attaining efficient service placement, which 
involves determining the ideal distribution of services 
across the distributed infrastructure to minimize latency, 
resource utilization, and operational costs while meeting 
application-specific requirements [12]. Service placement 
decisions directly impact the performance, reliability, and 
resource efficiency of fog/edge computing systems, making 
it a critical research area.
AI-based service placement is relevant to many real-
world settings with critical needs for latency, reliability, and 
resource use. In smart healthcare, for instance, placing AI 
services at the edge provides for real-time analysis of physi­
ological data from connected wearable devices in order to 
provide immediate and timely alerts in the event of cardiac 
arrest or suspicious falls. However, if all sensor data is sent 
to a distant cloud server, then it is impossible to provide 
immediate alerts, as the decision will incur considerable 
latency. In the area of autonomous vehicles and intelligent 
mobility systems, edge-based service placement allows 
for ultra-low latency communications between vehicular 
points (e.g. vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) communications) and 
vehicular infrastructure (e.g. vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I) 
communications) while making real-time, high-level deci­
sions to avoid collisions, reduce traffic flows, or manage and 
respond to constraints in dynamic routing [13]. In a similar 
way, Industry 4.0 and smart manufacturing utilize AI-based 
placement to facilitate predictive maintenance, robotic con­
trol, and automated processes where downtime or delayed 
decisions can really choke economic productivity. Smart 
City applications typically rely on good proximity to data 
sources, allowing AI services to be deployed close to data 
sources to ensure scalability and responsiveness in applica­
tions such as video surveillance, public safety using video 
footage, and intelligent energy distribution to residences and 
businesses. These practical realizations help to illustrate that 
service placement in fog and edge circumstances is not just 
a theoretical problem; it’s a dire necessity to facilitate next-
generation AI-powered services that will improve human 
safety, economic productivity, and the overall quality of life.
This paper presents an analysis of the service placement 
problem (SPP) in fog/edge computing environments. We 
aim to explore the underlying conditions, challenges, and 
state-of-the-art solutions in this domain. Through this sys­
tematic literature review, we attempt to offer insights into 
the current landscape of service placement in edge/fog com­
puting, identify research gaps, and highlight future research 
directions.

1.1  Evolution of computing paradigms
Computing is a goal-oriented activity that performs useful 
tasks. It is a very old term that has many shades. Particu­
larly in the field of computer science, it became one of the 
interesting research areas [14]. In this survey, we provide an 
evolution timeline of computing paradigms in Fig. 1
1.1.1  Distributed computing
Distributed computing fragments the job into several sub­
tasks to reduce the system’s complexity. It allows the sharing 
of available resources within the cluster of shared systems. 
If the load on one machine increases, then that load will be 
distributed to another machine, in such a way to achieve 
load balancing. Communication is possible via memory-
passing inter-process communication mechanisms. It is one 
of the traditional techniques for quick computing [15].
1.1.2  High-performance computing
It is a kind of parallel processing technique to overcome 
the complexities of processing huge volumes of data. This 
kind of computing is well-suited for high-level perfor­
mance computing scenarios [14]. Compared to distributed 
computing, it is high-speed in processing with low cost. It 
achieves maximum resource utilization and load balancing

1.1.3  Cloud computing
Cloud computing is one of the popular computing para­

somewhere else, called the cloud. Several services are

Another advantage of this computing type is that users need

they use. Today, billions of appliances are generating huge 
volumes of data that need to be processed in the cloud. So 
obviously, the workload on the cloud increased at times, and 
data needed to be processed at the premises of user.
1.1.4  Internet of things
Devices are interconnected using the internet, intended to 
communicate and exchange data [17]. All the devices are 
connected wirelessly and communicate with the help of pro­
tocols. Sensors and actuators are the basic examples of IoT 
devices at the device layer. Real-time monitoring of data, 
smart agriculture, smart cities, smart health, smart home, 
smart transportation, and forecasting are a few applications 
of IoT.
1.1.5  Fog computing
Fog computing is the enhancement of cloud computing 
which brings computation power and processing capabilities 
nearer to the end user premises [18]. It minimizes the dis­
tance between the user and the computing entity, hence 
latency will be greatly reduced by this computing facil­
ity. Moreover, localized servers, machines, and gateways 
enhance the performance of localized processing. Service 
placement and resource allocation needed to be done very 
efficiently for better performance of fog computing.
1.1.6  Edge computing
After 2011, edge computing gained much popularity by 
bringing processing, storage even nearer to the user. It is 
also an enhancement of cloud computing and fog comput­
ing. Sometimes fog computing and edge computing, these 
two terms are used interchangeably [19]. It enables the user 
to experience localized processing capability. Edge comput­
ing is a more efficient way in terms of reducing latency, and 
response time. Device identification and security of user 
content are critical and need to be implemented [20].
1.1.7  Serverless computing
By this emerging paradigm, developers can able to build 
applications without worrying about underlying infrastruc­
tures and servers [21]. The pricing models of serverless 
computing are based on actual execution time as well as 
resources used and this cuts costs for irregular workloads 
[22]. Common implementations of serverless computing are 
Amazon Web Services (AWS) Lambda, Azure Functions, 
and Google Cloud Functions [23].

1.3  Related Surveys
Many surveys and reviews are conducted on service place­
ment in fog/edge environment. Farah Ait Salah et al. [29] 
provided an overview of the Service Placement Problem 
(SPP) in Fog/Edge Computing to reflect its importance in 
the efficient deployment of IoT applications. Their paper 
proposed a new classification framework for categorizing 
research according to problem formulations, optimization 
goals, placement restrictions, and solution approaches. The 
study categorized five primary SPP scenarios based on user 
expectations and resource management complexity while 
comparing different methodologies, such as heuristic, meta­
heuristic, and AI-based approaches. It also investigated 
prominent optimization methods and experimental tools 
used for SPP solution evaluation. Moreover, the research 
outlined open issues such as scalability, dynamic resource 
allocation, security, energy efficiency, and real-time QoS 
provision, providing extensive insights into future research 
opportunities.
Sukhpal Singh et al. [41] carried out a comprehensive 
review on cloud resource scheduling, identifying issues like 
heterogeneity, uncertainty, and resource dispersion that the 
currently available allocation policies do not tackle. A litera­
ture review has broken down cloud resource scheduling into 
different aspects, such as scheduling algorithms, scheduling 
management, and resource distribution policies. The review 
has identified thirteen types of scheduling algorithms and 
eight types of resource distribution policies, namely work­
load-based, preemptive workloads, anticipatory workloads, 
and hold-out allocation policies, which will be described 
along with their advantages, tools, and effectiveness. There 
are two phases of cloud resource management: resource pro­
visioning- the allocation of a suitable number of resources 
based on QoS requirements, and resource scheduling- the 
mapping and execution of workload(s) run on the allocated 
resources in the cloud. Adaptive scheduling strategies are

to these areas of research are gaps in QoS-aware schedul­
ing techniques, which can help manage workloads, hence

1.1.8  Quantum computing
Quantum computing, which has come after cloud, fog, and 
edge computing as a powerful technology, indicates a shift 
in computational paradigms [24]. While cloud computing 
provides scalable and flexible resources through centralized 
data hubs, edge computing extends the processing power 
of data sources closer to the sources, and quantum comput­
ing introduces completely new methods of computation 
based on quantum mechanical principles [25]. Quantum 
computing uses qubits that can exist in multiple states at 
once (superposition) and can become entangled to allow for 
complex calculations that cannot be performed by classi­
cal systems at their speed [26]. This feature makes quantum 
computing particularly promising in solving cryptography, 
optimization, and beyond existing classical, even advanced 
edge or fog computing systems [27].
1.2  Motivation for conducting systematic literature 
review
The number of IoT devices is exponentially increasing day 
by day. These devices are producing huge amounts of data 
that need to be processed in the cloud. Traditional cloud 
computing techniques are not sufficient in modern days. 
Moreover, it increases the computation time, communica­
tion cost, and latency [28]. To overcome these issues, fog 
computing comes into existence. Fog computing brings 
computational resources near the users’ edge. Fog devices 
reside between edge nodes and the cloud, which consists 
of limited data processing capabilities. It is a challenging 
task to schedule the resources in a fog environment. Many 
researchers worked on this particular area to enhance the 
performance of fog computing. Service placement is one of 
the areas in resource scheduling that has a wide scope. It 
is also challenging to place the services between fog nodes 
because of mobility and heterogeneity in fog nodes. By con­
sidering all these facts, existing researchers worked on vari­
ous metrics like latency, energy efficiency, communication 
cost, network usage, and many more.
Recent research on service placement by Salaht et al. 
[29] provided service placement classification, optimization 
methods, deployment strategies, and scenarios that are well 
defined. More research on distributed, dynamic fog infra­
structure service placement is still on its way. Some fog 
nodes may move into another geographic location, or they 
may go into sleep mode or become unreachable. In this kind 
of situation, it is required to reallocate the services dynami­
cally. So, static methods or scheduling techniques are not 
enough to handle this scenario. Hence, automation comes 
into the picture. AI techniques and heuristics are provid­
ing better solutions to solve real-time difficulties in placing

1.5  Our contributions
We primarily focused on service placement optimization 
techniques and scenarios to address various issues related 
to fog computing environment. Primarily, we discussed fog 
computing characteristics and the idea of service placement. 
Then, we present the service placement classification and 
metrics. We partition the classification of the remaining 
paper as follows:

Service placement framework: This section deals with 
service placement concepts, optimization techniques, 
metrics, and deployment strategies.
	
●
Role of heuristics: It deals with different heuristic tech­
niques and their role in the optimal placement of ser­

●
Scenarios: This section deals with identified scenarios 
according to the latest research and trends. These sce­
narios’ comparisons with different simulation environ­
ments are expressed in a detailed manner.
We provide an extensive literature review of the recent 
approaches in the above sections. To do this, we considered

used as interchangeable concepts [56]. Fog computing 
operates between the device layer and the cloud layer. Fog 
computing serves as a distributed computing infrastructure 
that extends cloud capabilities to the proximity of the edge 
of the network. This paradigm facilitates the processing of 
data nearer to its source, minimizing latency and bandwidth 
usage while enhancing efficiency and responsiveness for 
various applications. Fog nodes possess contextual aware­
ness and are equipped with a unified data organization and 
communication system. They can be grouped into clusters, 
either vertically for isolation, horizontally for federation, or 
based on their proximity distance to smart end devices. [57]. 
Edge computing prioritizes bringing computing resources 
as near to the data source as feasible to minimize latency 
and bandwidth usage [58].

4.1.1  Static vs. Dynamic placement
Fog networks are highly dynamic in nature, and workload 
patterns are not predictable. Static placement involves the 
pre-allocation of services to specific fog nodes during the 
deployment phase. Once assigned, these placements typi­
cally remain fixed unless manually reconfigured. In the sce­
nario of dynamic service placement, workload patterns are 
varied based on time and demand. The system should adapt 
to these changes and should act accordingly. There should 
be dynamic scaling, and elastic features should be adopted 
in dynamic service placement. In a cloud gaming platform, 
static placement of the rendering service on an edge server 
near a metropolitan area guarantees predictable perfor­
mance for users located within that metropolitan area [80]. 
When user demand suddenly increases in another region 
where the service is statically placed, it will not be able to 
adapt automatically and will cause congestion and increased 
latency. Dynamic placement allows services to dynamically 
move at run time to follow demand. If, in the same scenario, 
a large number of players join from a suburban region, the 
rendering and streaming can be migrated to a nearby fog 
node which are underutilized.

The choice between online and offline placement depends 
on various factors such as application requirements, sys­
tem dynamics, resource constraints, and balancing between 
responsiveness versus predictability, as well as resource 
existing approaches into different categories. Each taxon­

provides a way to evaluate and compare approaches sys­

also classify the taxonomies of deployment strategy, archi­

4.1  Deployment strategy-based taxonomy
Fog computing deployment strategies determine how ser­
vices are assigned based on the dynamics of a fog comput­
ing system regarding expected workloads. Services can be 
placed statically, dynamically, and online, while the place­
ment is made offline. Static placement allocates services to 
particular nodes upon deployment, never to change unless 
manually reallocated by the user. On the other hand, after 
deployment, dynamic placement allows services to shift 
their assignments based on demand in near real-time [79]. 
In many ways, online placement follows the same method 
as dynamic placement and allows services to achieve fast 
assignment as needs are being made, meaning the demand 
for service is immediate while the assignment itself can take 
time (i.e., service assignment is made online). Conversely, 
when using offline placement of service, the placement of 
service relies on historical data and prediction models that 
pre-determine placements of services based on those predic­
tions. These deployment strategies can directly affect sys­
tem responsiveness, resource use, and efficiency.

4.2  Architectural taxonomy
The architectural taxonomy for service placements is cen­
tered on the decision-making process and resource distri­
bution across distributed systems. Centralized placement 
applies a single control entity to allocate resources, allow­
ing coordinated decision-making, but can present a single 
point of failure. Decentralized placement, on the other hand, 
delegates the decision-making process to multiple nodes to 
achieve improved fault tolerance and scalability. Macro-
level placement focuses on delivering services geographi­
cally as a decision at a high level, while micro placement is 
intended to improve resource allocation by managing fine-
grain task assignments more efficiently within local clusters.
4.2.1  Centralized vs. Decentralized placement
The reason why centralized placement is preferred is that, it 
makes it easy for management and coordination of resources, 
as decisions on where to place jobs can be made from a sin­
gle point. However, this strategy may lead to a single point 
of failure and increased latency. On the other hand, decen­
tralized placement allocates computational tasks to many 
different nodes within the fog network while not depending 
on any central coordinator, which results in improved fault 
tolerance and scalability. Decentralized placement is often 
good for applications that require high levels of resilience 
and scalability-IoT environments with many devices gener­
ating data [81, 82]. Some hybrid approaches exist whereby 
some tasks are placed at centers, whereas others are dis­
tributed across the network based on their specific require­
ments. Finally, the best placement strategy depends on the 
features as well as objectives of fog computing environment 
and its applications [59]. In smart healthcare monitoring, a 
centralized placement system collects patient information 
from various wearable devices, processes it at one central 
node. While it processes information concurrently, it may 
create delays in overall processing or a high risk for a sin­
gle point of failure for coordination. However, a decentral­
ized placement process runs on local fog nodes next to the 
patient, so latency is reduced, and fault tolerance provides 
essential functions for emergency response, such as the abil­
ity to detect an abnormal heart rhythm in real-time.

6.3.2  Simulated annealing (SA)
SA is a stochastic optimization algorithm motivated by 
annealing in metallurgy. In fog computing, simulated 
annealing can be used to optimize service placement as 
it involves allocating services to fog nodes based on the 
annealing process for close-to-best results. In this case, 
the simulated annealing optimization iteratively explores 
the solution space while occasionally agreeing to changes 
depending on a probability determined by a condition of 
acceptance. It allows escaping local minima and a more 
thorough search of the solution space, hence eventually 
nearing optimal solutions. To solve the problem of effective 
service placement in fog computing, one may use simulated 
annealing, where services are allocated to nodes with low 
latency and high resource utilization.
6.3.3  Particle swarm optimization (PSO)
PSO is a heuristic search algorithm that mimics the social 
behavior of birds flocking or fish schooling. In fog comput­
ing, PSO could be used to optimize service allocations to 
place the services on fog nodes through iterative updates 
of the positions of solution particles within a search space 
based on their own best position so far and the best posi­
tion found by other particles in the swarm. The process of 
optimization in PSO begins by initializing swarm particles 
in random positions and velocities within the search space. 
In this case, every particle represents an option where place­
ment is to be optimized, hence updating each particle’s posi­
tion toward finding an optimal solution.
At each iteration, there is movement of particles due to 
positioning information acquired so far by these individu­
als and also from those that are within the whole group. 
It involves adjusting their locations based on what others 
know, even as they move towards better placement solu­
tions over iterations.
In fog computing infrastructure, PSO can offer solu­
tions to how efficient services can be placed by optimizing 
the allocation of services to different fog nodes taking into 
account parameters like latency, resource utilization, and 
new service deployment strategies.

6.3.5  Ant colony optimization (ACO)
ACO is a meta-heuristic approach inspired by nature. This 
algorithm evolved based on simulating the behavior of ants 
looking for food which helps allocate services to fog nodes 
to optimize the system. The ACO optimization process aims 
at mimicking pheromone deposition and trails following 
procedures existing in real ant colonies. In service place­
ment, potential solution paths are trails that are iteratively 
constructed and updated by artificial ants based on how 
good the solutions’ quality is.
In ACO, artificial ants build solutions by probabilisti­
cally choosing paths according to the deposited amount of 
pheromone and the desirability of the paths selected. The 
constructed solutions quality updates are used to adjust 
the pheromone trails, thus until near-optimal solutions are 
reached.

service placement problems by optimizing which services 
should be allocated to each fog node according to different

11.1  Future research directions
Looking forward, research along the SPP (Service Place­
ment Problem) in fog/edge computation must advance from 
static and simplistic assumptions of operation operating in 
highly dynamic, heterogeneous, and resource-constrained 
environments. Cases involving ultra-low power IoT devices, 
mobility-aware service placement, and edge nodes mounted 
on UAV or mobile devices offer real-world cases. Design 
context-aware and adaptive placement methods capable of 
handling not only user demands, but also varying network 
conditions and energy budgets, are most important. Feder­
ated learning, decentralized AI models, and lightweight deep 
reinforcement learning will be influential in enabling these 
methods in a distributed and privacy-preserving manner, 
while service placement should evolve to multi-objective 
optimization, jointly considering latency, energy-efficiency, 
service availability, and user experience.
Emerging technologies such as Federated Learning and 
Quantum AI (QAI) present opportunities to improve service 
placement in fog and edge environments [24]. FL allows 
for training models in a decentralized manner and preserves 
privacy by training on distributed nodes. This allows for 
placement decisions to be made near the data while retain­
ing privacy, instead of transferring sensitive information 
to regional or cloud infrastructures. FL also lowers com­
munication traffic overhead and can provide the basis for 
context-aware and adaptive service placement, particularly 
in dynamically changing environments, such as healthcare,

the expanding fog and edge ecosystem.
10  Research gaps
This survey provides a comprehensive review of the cur­
rent state of art and practice in service placement for fog 
computing and more broadly for edge computing. Neverthe­
less, there are some research gaps that could be considered 
in future studies. Most of the existing studies focus on fog 
computing, which is a special case of edge computing that 
deals with data collection from IoT sensors. There is a lack 
of studies that consider the placement of services in edge 
and fog computing that deal with very dynamic and hetero­
geneous scenarios, such as a large number of IoT sensors 
with ultra-low power consumption and very limited battery 
capacity, or mobile fog nodes deployed on Unmanned Aerial 
Vehicles (UAVs). Moreover, there is no standard evaluation 
metric or benchmark dataset to evaluate the performance of 
the existing and future service placement algorithms in fog 
and edge computing. Additionally, more research is required 
to develop context-aware and adaptive service placement 
algorithms that can make dynamic decisions in the presence 
of varying network conditions and user demands [194]. Fur­
thermore, the impact of security and privacy constraints and 
energy efficiency criteria on service placement decisions 
can be an intriguing research direction. Ultimately, this sur­
vey opens up promising research avenues in the field of ser­
vice placement for edge computing.

Abstract: Fog and edge computing bring computational resources closer to end users, which is necessary for the rapid growth of applications that are latency-sensitive and bandwidth-intensive. The service placement is a significant issue since optimiz­ ing it depends on several dynamic variables, including the network’s topology, heterogeneity, and available resources. These issues are challenging due to their high level of complexity, which is why Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven solu­ tions are so appealing. In this article, we present a systematic literature review for service placement strategies in fog and edge computing environments that use heuristic optimization, reinforcement learning, and deep learning for optimization. Further, we propose a comprehensive taxonomy to thoroughly categorize and evaluate current methods according to per­ formance indicators like energy usage, latency reduction, network utilization, quality of service, and general workload flexibility. Additionally, this work establishes a correlation between metric priority and methodological trends throughout the research period. One of our main contributions is the methodical categorization and critical evaluation of heuristic approaches, which shows how they are changing in their ability to balance computational efficiency and solution quality, especially in dynamic, large-scale edge contexts and multi-objective optimization. This paper acts as a guide for profes­ sionals and practitioners in the rapidly evolving field of AI-based service placement solutions and highlights new direc­ tions to help define future research topics.
